flashcards.back: Raised when a delegate experiences personal discomfort that impairs participation (e.g. audibility, temperature). May interrupt a speaker.
Raised when a delegate believes the Chair or a delegate has improperly followed the rules of procedure. May interrupt a speaker only if the error is urgent.
A question to the Chair about the rules of procedure. Cannot interrupt a speaker.
A question to a speaker who has yielded to points of information. Must be phrased as a question.
Requested when a delegate's national integrity has been impugned by another delegate. Granted at the Chair's discretion.
Begins formal debate on the agenda. Requires a simple majority.
Chooses which topic is discussed first. Typically two speakers for, two against; simple majority.
Must specify total time, speaking time, and purpose. Simple majority. The Chair calls on speakers.
Must specify total time. Delegates move freely to negotiate and draft. Simple majority.
Ends debate and moves into voting procedure. Usually two speakers against; requires a two-thirds majority.
Suspends debate on the current topic. Usually requires a two-thirds majority.
Pauses the session (e.g. for lunch). Simple majority.
Ends the session for the conference. Usually only in the final session; simple majority.

flashcards.front: Motion to Introduce a Draft Resolution
flashcards.back: Brings a draft resolution onto the floor once it has the required number of sponsors/signatories and Chair approval.
An amendment agreed to by all sponsors; incorporated without a vote.
An amendment not supported by all sponsors; requires signatories and a committee vote.
The speaker gives remaining time back to the Chair.
Remaining time is given to another delegate, who may not yield further.
The speaker accepts questions from delegates for the remaining time.
Motion to vote on operative clauses of a resolution separately. Procedural vote on how to divide.
Each delegate votes aloud when called: Yes, No, Abstain, Pass (or 'with rights').
The minimum number of members present to conduct business - often one-third to begin debate, a majority to vote on substance.
Sponsors authored and support the resolution; signatories only wish to see it debated and need not vote for it.
Simple majority: more than half of members present and voting. Qualified (two-thirds): needed for cloture and some procedural motions.
A short question or statement offered to the opposing speaker during unprotected time. The speaker may accept or decline; accept 1-2 per speech.
The first and last minute of a speech (BP, Asians, WSDC) when POIs may not be offered. Marked by a single knock or bell.
What a side must prove to win. Usually set by the motion's wording and the definitions: e.g. 'This House would' requires a policy and its benefits.
The Proposition's concrete policy mechanism: who does what, how it is enforced and funded. Opposition may challenge but should not 'squirrel' the debate.
Defining the motion in an unreasonable or unexpected way to escape the core clash. Penalised by adjudicators.
An alternative policy the Opposition proposes instead of the status quo. It must be mutually exclusive with the Proposition's model.
The core points of disagreement between the sides. Good speakers identify 2-3 clashes and win them explicitly.
Comparing impacts to show why your arguments matter more: magnitude, probability, timeframe, reversibility, and who is affected.
New material from a closing team that is distinct from its opening half and adds a new reason to win. Required to beat the opening team.
BP closing half: the Member brings the extension; the Whip summarises the debate by clashes and may not add new arguments.
A biased summary by the 1st or 2nd speaker, Opposition first. No new arguments; shows why your side won the key clashes.
An argument the other side never responded to. Point it out: in most formats it is treated as conceded.
A 3-minute period where both speakers question each other. Grand crossfire involves all four debaters.
A 3-minute question period where the previous speaker is questioned by an opponent. Used to set up arguments, not to make speeches.
The value is the ideal the resolution should be judged by (e.g. justice); the criterion is the standard for measuring whether that value is achieved.
A quoted passage with a tag (the claim it proves) and a full citation. Used in PF, LD and Policy; paraphrasing a card misrepresents evidence.
Telling the judge where you are: 'I have two responses, then my extension.' It makes the flow easy to follow.
Individual scores (e.g. 50-100 in BP, 60-80 in WSDC, 25-30 in US formats) reflecting style, content and strategy.
